hero.headline: AAA expects 4 million Floridians to drive during Fourth of July weekend as traffic fatalities spike 44% on holiday
hero.body:
Nearly 4.6 million Floridians are expected to travel at least 50 miles from home during the Fourth of July weekend, representing a 3% increase from the previous year. About 4 million of these travelers will drive, while an additional 330,000 will fly and roughly 204,000 will use buses, trains, cruises, or other transportation methods. As one of the nation's top domestic travel destinations, Florida will experience significant traffic congestion on major highways including I-4, I-95, and roads leading to beaches and theme parks. Travel timing matters during this busy period. AAA and INRIX data recommend that drivers avoid afternoon and evening travel, particularly on July 2 when people are heading out and on July 5 and 6 when they return home. Early morning hours generally offer the best driving conditions.

The statistics surrounding holiday traffic safety paint a concerning picture. On a typical July day, Florida experiences an average of 7 to 8 traffic fatalities. However, the Fourth of July itself has historically produced a 44% spike in fatalities, averaging about 11 deaths on that single day based on data from 2017 through 2021. Throughout entire holiday weekends, the state has seen between 25 and 32 or more deaths, with many of these accidents linked to alcohol impairment and failure to use seatbelts.

Vehicle maintenance plays a critical role in preventing accidents during holiday travel. Benny Garcia at Palm Beach Tire Pros emphasizes the importance of checking tire pressure before long drives. To determine if tires need replacement, drivers can use the penny test by placing a coin upside down in the tire treads. If you can see the entire outline of Abraham Lincoln's head, the tires should be changed. Understanding tire age is equally important. The date code on a tire's sidewall provides this information, with the first two numbers indicating the week of manufacture and the last two numbers showing the year. Most tires typically last between 5 and 6 years.

Before embarking on Fourth of July travel, drivers should perform a complete vehicle inspection. Check tire pressure, battery condition, and all fluid levels, including oil. Pack an emergency kit in your vehicle in case of unexpected problems. Once on the road, maintaining focus is essential for safety. Put away your phone and eliminate distractions. Remember that fatigued driving poses dangers similar to impaired driving. By taking these precautions and planning your travel schedule carefully, you can help ensure a safer holiday weekend for yourself and your family.

cards.headline: Supreme Court Ruling Allows End to Protected Status for 350,000 Haitian Refugees, Nearly Half in Florida
cards.body:
The Supreme Court's 6-3 decision has cleared the way for the Department of Homeland Security to end temporary protected status for 350,000 Haitians across the country. Within hours of the ruling, Rep. Frederica Wilson of Miami-Dade responded by introducing the Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act in the House. The bill would create a pathway to green cards for eligible Haitian nationals who have lived in the United States since June 26, 2024, as well as their family members.

Florida will experience the effects of this decision more than any other state. According to the National Immigration Forum, approximately 404,000 TPS holders currently live in Florida, significantly more than Texas with roughly 147,000. The Migration Policy Institute reports that nearly half of all Haitians in the United States, about 49 percent, live in Florida. The Supreme Court's ruling affects Haitians who have been living legally in the country for years, many of whom registered, paid required fees, worked, paid taxes, and established roots in their communities.

Wilson, who has represented Miami-Dade for more than four decades, called the Supreme Court decision heartbreaking but emphasized that Congress retains the power to protect these families. She stated that her bill would move Haitian families from uncertainty to stability, and that TPS was never meant to become a lifetime of uncertainty. Her bill already has support from other Florida Democrats, including Reps. Maxwell Frost of Orlando and Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Broward County, who became original co-sponsors. In April, the House previously passed a separate bill to extend TPS for Haitians through a discharge petition, which received support from 10 Republicans including South Florida representatives Mario Diaz-Balart, Carlos Gimenez, and Maria Elvira Salazar.

The path forward in the Senate presents a more significant challenge. Any legislation will require 60 votes to advance, a difficult threshold even with leadership backing. Wilson argued that her bill creates a responsible pathway to lawful permanent resident status while maintaining safeguards to protect public safety. She emphasized that Haitian families have complied with legal requirements and strengthened communities by working and paying taxes. The Supreme Court's decision puts hundreds of thousands of Haitian families at risk of deportation after years of legal residence in the United States.

cards.headline: DEA lab in Miami reports alarming increase in fentanyl and carfentanil in Florida drug samples
cards.teaser: Forensic chemists at the DEA's busiest drug lab in Miami are seeing frightening amounts of fentanyl and carfentanil in recent drug samples, with some testing as high as 16% fentanyl concentration.
cards.body:
The DEA's Miami drug lab, the busiest in the nation, is detecting disturbing quantities of fentanyl and carfentanil in seized drug samples. Chemist Alyssa Sanchez, who has worked at the facility for three years, expressed concern about the trend. "I see a lot of fentanyl, but even more recently I've seen a lot of carfentanil in my samples; it's scary," she said. The Miami lab's prominent role stems from its coastal location and proximity to South America, making it a critical testing facility for drugs entering the United States. Sanchez recently analyzed a kilogram brick of fentanyl that tested at approximately 16 percent purity and also contained carfentanil, a substance thousands of times more potent than fentanyl itself.

Fentanyl is a powerful synthetic opioid used medically to treat pain, but it has become the leading cause of death for Americans ages 18 to 45. The drug is 100 times stronger than morphine and 50 times stronger than heroin. Just two milligrams, roughly the size of a salt grain, can be lethal. Carfentanil has no approved use for humans and exists solely as a tranquilizer for large animals like elephants. A single kilogram brick containing fentanyl at the concentrations Sanchez discovered could kill thousands of people. When asked about the potency level, Sanchez confirmed that 16 percent concentration is considered high for fentanyl samples.

According to Miles Aley, special agent in charge of the DEA's Miami Division, Mexican drug cartels have shifted toward using carfentanil after the Chinese government restricted precursor chemicals needed to manufacture fentanyl. The cartels have sourced both chemicals and expertise through the dark web to enhance the potency of their drugs. Aley emphasized that the agency considers fentanyl and carfentanil a top priority. He noted that while overdose deaths have declined from 110,000 annually to 70,000, this reduction does not necessarily reflect decreased drug use. Instead, more people are surviving overdoses thanks to Narcan, an over-the-counter nasal spray that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The DEA plans to address the crisis through its inaugural Fentanyl Free America Summit scheduled for next month in Orlando, designed to increase public awareness about the current fentanyl emergency. Aley also warned about emerging drugs that resist Narcan treatment. These new compounds represent a different chemical structure that renders Narcan ineffective against overdoses. Aley acknowledged that solving the fentanyl crisis requires sustained effort from multiple organizations and agencies, with no single solution available.

cards.headline: Supreme Court ruling eliminates protected status for Haitians and Syrians, impacting thousands in South Florida
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration to eliminate Temporary Protected Status for people from Haiti and Syria, leaving roughly 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians nationwide at risk of deportation.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court has sided with President Donald Trump's administration in eliminating Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria, leaving hundreds of thousands at risk of deportation. The ruling impacts roughly 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians nationwide, including many in South Florida. According to the Migration Policy Institute, Florida has the largest Haitian immigrant population in the United States, with Palm Beach County ranking third nationally at 68,400 Haitian immigrants, behind Broward County's 86,100 and Miami-Dade County's 78,800. Temporary Protected Status allows foreign citizens already in the United States to stay, work, and raise their families while their home countries deal with turmoil from natural disasters, political unrest, or violence.

In Riviera Beach, restaurant owner Stecko Dulcio, a U.S. citizen, expressed concern for friends with TPS, calling the decision "a disaster." He noted that gangs have taken over Haiti, claiming houses, controlling transportation, and fueling violence. Attorney Byrnes Guillaume, who is Haitian and represents many people in danger of losing TPS, explained that eliminating TPS means people have no status, cannot work legally, and must "go in the shadow," despite potentially having American-born children. Guillaume stated, "I do think lives will be at risk." No timeline on deportations has been set.

cards.teaser: A Vero Beach man faces murder charges in his grandmother's death following a monthslong investigation.

A Vero Beach man was charged with his grandmother's murder after a monthslong investigation. The arrest comes after authorities spent months investigating the case.

The case has been ongoing for several months before charges were filed. The man is now in custody facing murder charges in connection with his grandmother's death.

cards.headline: Lightning strikes spark multiple brush fires across Martin County
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to multiple brush fires across the county on Friday following powerful lightning strikes. Fire rescue crews joined deputies in battling the blazes throughout the area.

The lightning activity created hazardous conditions as multiple fires ignited across Martin County. Video captured the intensity of the lightning strikes that preceded the brush fire outbreak.

Both the Martin County Sheriff's Office and fire rescue teams mobilized to address the fires. The incidents occurred as powerful weather moved through the region.

The fires were attributed to natural lightning strikes rather than human causes. Authorities worked throughout the day to contain the multiple brush fires sparked by the severe weather.

cards.headline: Woman charged with aggravated battery after striking mother with hammer near Sebastian
cards.body:
A woman faces an aggravated battery charge after allegedly striking her mother with a hammer near Sebastian, according to authorities.

The incident occurred in an area near Sebastian in Indian River County. The woman was taken into custody and charged with aggravated battery following the assault on her mother.

Aggravated battery is a felony charge in Florida that typically involves the use of a deadly weapon or results in serious bodily harm. The hammer used in the alleged attack qualifies as a weapon under state law.

The investigation into the incident is being handled by local law enforcement. The woman remains in custody facing the felony charge.

cards.headline: Orlando Health opens new primary care facility in Vero Beach to address Indian River County doctor shortage
cards.teaser: Orlando Health held a ribbon-cutting Thursday for its new eight-exam-room adult primary healthcare center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Orlando Health held a ribbon-cutting Thursday for its new eight-exam-room adult primary healthcare center at 3745 11th Circle, Suite 101, in Vero Beach. The facility can accommodate 40 patients a day and has room to grow, according to Aaron Bridges, assistant vice president of Orlando Health. The center will be led by husband-and-wife physicians Dr. Meron Kristos and Dr. Gabitto, who met during residency at the former St. Vincent's hospital in New York City. According to the Cleveland Clinic, Indian River County is designated a health professional shortage area and medically underserved area.

Dr. Kristos said the shortage has created extended wait times, with people waiting months for primary care appointments. Christine Stenback, who has lived in Indian River County for nearly three decades, said the shortage has affected her since she moved to the area with her daughter. At that time, there were few primary care physicians and no specialists, so she and her daughter retained doctors in Fort Lauderdale and traveled there for care. Kristos said the new facility aims to provide quick appointment times for patients to get established and have access to care when needed, helping reduce wait times and address primary care shortages throughout Indian River County.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast entrepreneur proposes buying Spirit Airlines and rebasing it in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: LeRoy Gillead II has proposed buying all of Spirit Airlines, rehiring the airline's workers and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach.
cards.body:
Spirit Airlines is in bankruptcy court liquidating its assets, including planes, airport gates and potentially its headquarters. A Treasure Coast entrepreneur, LeRoy Gillead II, has proposed acquiring the airline and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost carrier based in West Palm Beach. According to court papers, Gillead is seeking up to $250 million from private investors to complete the acquisition. The deadline for bids is in July.

Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, expressed skepticism about the proposal. "This seems like a pie in the sky thing. If they can get the money together, maybe they'll establish a new low-cost carrier, but right now they don't fly any routes at all," Henderson said. He predicted the airline's assets would more likely be divided among the highest bidders, probably major airlines. Henderson added that the low-cost carrier model is struggling in the U.S., with all such carriers struggling to make money. He advised consumers to be "airline agnostic" and use tools like Google Flights to find the cheapest fares rather than remaining loyal to a single airline.

cards.headline: Boca Raton psychiatrist's license suspended after patients allege he asked them to undress on Zoom
cards.teaser: Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo issued an emergency suspension of Dr. Andrew Sorial's medical license after at least two patients say they were asked to undress during telehealth sessions.
cards.body:
A Boca Raton psychiatrist is facing serious allegations after at least two patients say they were asked to undress during mental health appointments conducted via telehealth. Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo issued an emergency suspension of Dr. Andrew Sorial's medical license following the allegations. According to state documents, a 29-year-old patient identified as S.A. began treatment with Sorial in 2020 for depression, anxiety and OCD. During a Zoom appointment, the woman discussed body image concerns when Sorial allegedly asked to assess her body and eventually requested she strip down to a bra and underwear. In another visit, the patient was allegedly asked to take off her top and show him her breasts. State documents include this exchange: Patient S.A. asked Sorial if he was asking her to take her top off and show him her naked breasts. Sorial said, "yes, if that's what you're comfortable with."

Around summer of 2025, another patient, a 33-year-old woman identified as C.B., saw Sorial for ADHD, depression and bipolar disorder. State documents allege similar requests over Zoom, escalating to providing photos of the patient in a bra, underwear or bikini. A lawsuit has been filed against Sorial and Boca Raton Psychiatry. WPTV sought a response from Sorial and the practice but did not receive one. No criminal charges have been filed. Palm Beach County Victim Services operates a 24-hour crisis helpline at 561-833-7273, or toll-free at 866-891-7273 for those outside the local calling area.

cards.headline: SoFlo Market plans Independence Day celebration at Boca Raton City Hall on July 4
cards.teaser: The popular SoFlo Market will turn Boca Raton City Hall into a hub of red, white and blue celebration this Independence Day with family activities, local vendors and patriotic entertainment.
cards.body:
Tatiana Freitas, founder and organizer of SoFlo Market, is planning an Independence Day celebration at Boca Raton City Hall on Saturday, July 4 from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. The free event will feature patriotic activities including a kids' parade, a DJ, unique vendors, gourmet food, and free gifts for the first 20 children through the gate. Freitas said the market's mission is to uplift small local businesses and bring the community together. The event will take place at Boca Raton City Hall, 201 West Palmetto Park Road.

Visitors can expect face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, and balloon twisting alongside the market's signature handmade crafts and desserts. A live appearance by the SoFlo Market's flamingo mascot is planned as a crowd favorite. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to participate. Kyle, Freitas' son, and Eddie, her husband, are part of the organizing team. While the SoFlo Market runs monthly, Freitas said the Independence Day edition is always a standout.

hero.headline: West Palm Beach entrepreneur bids to buy Spirit Airlines, rebrand as Florida Air Express
hero.teaser: A Treasure Coast entrepreneur has proposed buying Spirit Airlines and rebranding it as a low-cost carrier based in West Palm Beach, but industry experts are skeptical the deal will happen.
hero.body:
LeRoy Gillead II, a Treasure Coast entrepreneur, has submitted a proposal to purchase Spirit Airlines in its entirety, rehire its workforce, and relaunch the company as Florida Air Express, a low-cost carrier headquartered in West Palm Beach. According to court documents filed during Spirit's bankruptcy proceedings, Gillead is seeking to raise approximately $250 million from private investors to fund the acquisition. The deadline for all bids is scheduled for July.

The bankruptcy sale includes Spirit's valuable assets such as aircraft, airport gates, and potentially its headquarters building. Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, expressed doubt about whether Gillead's plan will come to fruition. Henderson believes it is far more probable that Spirit's assets will be distributed to the highest bidders, which are likely to be major established airlines rather than a new startup carrier. "This seems like a pie in the sky thing. If they can get the money together, maybe they'll establish a new low-cost carrier, but right now they don't fly any routes at all," Henderson said.

The disappearance of Spirit Airlines marks a significant shift in the budget travel market, leaving fewer options for cost-conscious passengers. Many travelers relied on Spirit for affordable fares during a time when travel expenses continue to rise. Henderson noted that the low-cost carrier model faces serious challenges in the United States, with existing budget airlines struggling to maintain profitability. Currently, only Frontier and Allegiant remain operating as low-cost carriers in the industry.

For consumers seeking affordable airfare following Spirit's collapse, Henderson recommends a flexible approach rather than airline loyalty. "Be airline agnostic; that's the best advice I have for consumers," Henderson said. "Go with the cheapest airline you can find. Use Google Flights and don't try to be loyal to one airline." This strategy requires travelers to invest additional time comparing prices across carriers but increases the likelihood of finding the best available fares. The Spirit Airlines bankruptcy signals broader challenges facing budget air travel in the United States, and the eventual fate of its distinctive yellow aircraft remains uncertain as they await potential repainting in new company colors.

cards.headline: George Snow Scholarship Fund in Boca Raton awards record $7.5 million to local students
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton-based scholarship fund awarded more than $7.5 million to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, the largest amount in its 40-year history.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded a record $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, according to President Tim Snow. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. Snow said the program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

The fund's services extend beyond financial aid to include mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast, noted Vice President of Development Jay Brandt. One recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University. The organization also operates the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which provides professional, formal, and casual clothing to scholars for interviews, internships, and campus life.

cards.headline: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers trade certifications to residents
cards.teaser: West Tech provides programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other trades, working with community and business partners to help people find work in Belle Glade and surrounding areas.
cards.body:
West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers trade training and certifications for high school students and adults seeking to learn skills that lead to employment. According to Adrian Dowdell with the education center, West Tech operates programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other trades. The center works with community and business partners to help people find work in Belle Glade and surrounding communities.

The education center recently promoted its programs at a Let's Hear It meet-up at the library in Belle Glade using a mobile unit to spread awareness about available training opportunities in the area.

cards.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner's mother survives Venezuela earthquake building collapse
cards.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, learned his mother was trapped under rubble after her building collapsed in the 7.5 magnitude quake.
cards.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, learned of two powerful earthquakes in Venezuela measured at 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes through news alerts. When video arrived showing the building where his mother lived, he feared the worst. Hours later, his brother confirmed she had been inside when it collapsed. Communication in Venezuela was severed due to power outages, leaving Peroza in anguish for about eight hours until a call arrived around 3 a.m. confirming his mother was alive but trapped under rubble. Relatives and neighbors worked with bare hands to free her. She sustained a broken hip and requires surgery, and lost her home in the collapse.

Peroza described Venezuela as unprepared for a disaster of this magnitude, lacking the equipment and infrastructure needed for rescue and recovery efforts. He said the U.S. has committed to sending crews to help. Officials confirm nearly 200 people are dead and at least 1,000 others are injured. Peroza believes he can provide more assistance from Florida than traveling to the disaster zone, and plans to continue operating his food truck while advocating for his country's needs. He described his mother's survival as "absolutely a miracle" and called for urgent international humanitarian assistance including rescue teams, medical support, and equipment.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County has third-largest Haitian population in U.S. as TPS protections end
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County is home to 68,400 Haitian immigrants, ranking third in the state and nation, as the Supreme Court sides with the Trump administration to eliminate Temporary Protected Status for Haiti and Syria.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County is home to 68,400 Haitian immigrants, ranking third in the United States behind Broward County's 86,100 and Miami-Dade County's 78,800, according to the Migration Policy Institute. The Supreme Court sided with President Donald Trump's administration to eliminate Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. The ruling impacts roughly 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians nationwide, with no timeline on deportations yet established.

Stecko Dulcio, who has operated a Haitian restaurant in Riviera Beach for five and a half years, called the end of TPS "a disaster" for the community. Though a U.S. citizen himself, Dulcio said Haiti is too dangerous, with gangs taking over houses, controlling transportation, and fueling violence. Attorney Byrnes Guillaume, who represents many people facing TPS elimination, said losing the status means individuals have no legal standing, can no longer work, and must "go in the shadow." Guillaume highlighted the burden on families with American-born children, questioning whether they would leave their children in the U.S. or take them to Haiti, a country they have never known. "I do think lives will be at risk," Guillaume said.

cards.headline: Former Haitian national team players hold soccer clinic in Boca Raton
cards.teaser: L'Union Fait La Force Training Center, run by former Haitian National Team members including former captain Jean-Marc Alexandre, hosted a clinic from June 25-28 for youth players.
cards.body:
Former members of the Haitian national soccer team mentored young players in Boca Raton this week, days after a Wednesday night match against Morocco. The L'Union Fait La Force Training Center hosted a clinic from June 25-28 to provide players a pathway to the youth national team. Jean-Marc Alexandre, a former Haiti national team captain and Atlantic High School and Lynn University graduate, runs the program. Alexandre was a member of Real Salt Lake's 2009 MLS Cup-winning team. "The whole purpose of this camp is to give these kids a pathway to the youth national team, being that they're not living in Haiti, so we give opportunities to the next generation," Alexandre said.

Nohe Chevry, one of the young participants, moved to Palm Beach County from Haiti in 2022 with his family for safety reasons. "Haiti was in a bad state, so for safety we just moved here," Chevry said. After arriving, he sought out a local soccer team and joined the training center. "It's a great opportunity to learn; they've been through all of the soccer stuff, pro contracts, so they can teach us, and it's really kind of them to do that," Chevry said. Another participant, Luis Etienne, expressed gratitude for the exposure opportunity. "It's nice that they're giving us the opportunity to come out here and give us this opportunity to potentially get some exposure for the national team," Etienne said.

hero.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner says mother survived Venezuela earthquake building collapse
hero.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, said his mother was pulled from rubble after her building collapsed in two powerful earthquakes in Venezuela.
hero.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods, a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, describes his business as more than just a place to eat. "This is a cultural Venezuelan experience that we share with the community. We call it Venezuela without a passport," he said. That connection to his homeland became deeply personal when two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes struck Venezuela seconds apart. Peroza first learned of the disaster through news alerts, but the reality hit hard when he saw video footage of the building where his mother lived. Hours later, his brother confirmed she had been inside when the structure collapsed around 3 a.m.

Communication in Venezuela became nearly impossible as power failed and connections were cut. Peroza spent anxious hours not knowing if his mother was alive, relying on prayer to maintain peace. After about eight hours, the call finally came confirming she had survived. His relatives and neighbors had worked with their bare hands to free her from the rubble. "The Venezuelan culture is well known because of the service for the people, and especially in this kind of situation," Peroza said. His mother suffered a broken hip requiring surgery and lost her home in the collapse in the coastal state of La Guaira.

The disaster revealed a wider humanitarian crisis affecting the entire region. Peroza described a population struggling without power, water, or shelter. Officials confirm nearly 200 people are dead and at least 1,000 others are injured. Most buildings are made of concrete and metal, making rescue efforts extremely difficult with limited tools. "The country doesn't have any structure for this kind of situation," Peroza said. "We need international help immediately." The United States announced it would send rescue crews to assist. Peroza emphasized the urgency of the situation, noting that survivors face unclear prospects for food, work, and shelter in the coming days.

Despite the disaster affecting his family, Peroza believes he can help more effectively from Florida than by traveling to Venezuela. "We don't have any plans to go down there. I think we are more helpful from here," he explained, noting that his mother and other survivors will need housing and resources that require commercial activity and employment opportunities. He plans to continue operating his food truck while raising awareness about Venezuela's needs. Peroza called his mother's rescue "absolutely a miracle" and said it proves more lives can still be saved with international response. "There are families in Venezuela waiting for rescue, medical attention, information, and hope," he said. "Right now, Venezuela needs urgent humanitarian help."

cards.headline: Former Haiti national team captain runs soccer training center in Boca Raton
cards.teaser: Jean-Marc Alexandre, former Haiti national team captain and Atlantic High School graduate, operates L'Union Fait La Force Training Center in Boca Raton to give young Haitian players a pathway to the youth national team.
cards.body:
Jean-Marc Alexandre, former captain of the Haitian national soccer team, runs L'Union Fait La Force Training Center in Boca Raton. An Atlantic High School and Lynn University graduate, Alexandre was a member of Real Salt Lake's 2009 MLS Cup-winning team. From June 25-28, the training center hosted a clinic teaching top-level Haitian soccer players. "The whole purpose of this camp is to give these kids a pathway to the youth national team, being that they're not living in Haiti, so we give opportunities to the next generation," Alexandre said. The clinic took place days after Haiti's Wednesday night match against Morocco.

Young players attended the clinic seeking exposure for Haiti's national team. Nohe Chevry, who moved to Palm Beach County from Haiti in 2022 for safety reasons, participated in the training. "It's a great opportunity to learn; they've been through all of the soccer stuff, pro contracts, so they can teach us, and it's really kind of them to do that," Chevry said. Luis Etienne also attended the clinic. "It's nice that they're giving us the opportunity to come out here and give us this opportunity to potentially get some exposure for the national team," Etienne said.

cards.headline: Breeze Airways adds 5 new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport with fares starting at $79
cards.teaser: Breeze Airways announced Wednesday five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport with one-way fares starting at $79.
cards.body:
Breeze Airways announced five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport on Wednesday, offering one-way fares starting at $79. Travelers can book nonstop flights to Atlantic City, New Jersey on Mondays and Fridays beginning October 2 from $89 one way, and to Baltimore on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays starting October 1 from $79 one way. Nonstop service to Trenton, New Jersey begins September 30 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, switching to Thursdays and Sundays beginning January 7, from $89 one way.

Breeze will also offer one-stop, no-change-of-plane BreezeThru service to Burlington, Vermont on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays starting October 4, and to Provo, Utah on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays beginning October 2. The additions follow recent service expansions at Vero Beach Regional Airport. JetBlue began service to Boston and New York's JFK airports in December 2024, and American Airlines began service to Charlotte in February 2025. Breeze Airways currently operates more than 300 year-round and seasonal routes to 91 cities in the United States, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Zoo reveals first koala joey is a boy
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach Zoo announced their first-ever koala joey born on site is a boy. The joey was born in September to mother Elin and is starting to explore the expanded koala habitat.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach Zoo announced Thursday that their first-ever koala joey born on site is a boy. Animal Experience Curator Mike Terrell shared the news at the koala habitat. Born in September no bigger than a jelly bean, the joey immediately crawled into his mother Elin's pouch where he has been growing for months. Terrell said the joey is starting to explore and spends most of his time on his mother's back, often keeping an arm connected to her for safety as he cautiously ventures into the world.

The timing of the birth coincides with the Palm Beach Zoo's unveiling of an expanded koala habitat featuring a climate-controlled indoor forest with solar tubes for natural lighting and carefully designed perching areas. The koalas in North America are on loan from the Australian federal government as part of a conservation program facilitated by San Diego Zoo Global. Terrell emphasized that zoo visitors directly support conservation efforts for wild koalas simply by visiting. As the joey continues to grow more independent, he is expected to ride on his mother's back closer to summer.

cards.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund headquartered in Boca Raton awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, President Tim Snow said. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. Snow said the program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford, offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

Beyond financial assistance, the fund provides mentorship, professional development and resources like the College Compass podcast, according to Vice President of Development Jay Brandt. The Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, offers professional, formal and casual wear for scholars attending interviews, internships and campus activities. Donations include new or gently used clothing, footwear and accessories. Wellington Community High School graduate Zya Chow received both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University.

cards.headline: West Technical Education Center offers trade certifications in Belle Glade
cards.teaser: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other trades to help high school students and adults get certifications that lead to work.
cards.body:
West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade provides training programs for high school students and adults looking to learn trades and get certifications that lead to work, according to Adrian Dowdell with the education center. The center was promoting programs at a recent library meet-up in Belle Glade.

Dowdell said West Tech has programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other trades. The center works with community and business partners to help people find work in Belle Glade and surrounding communities. The education center brought a truck to spread the word about available programs.

cards.headline: Spirit Airlines bankruptcy leaves travelers with fewer low-cost options from Florida airports
cards.teaser: Spirit Airlines is in bankruptcy court to sell off planes, airport gates and potentially its headquarters. A Treasure Coast entrepreneur has proposed buying Spirit and rebranding it as Florida Air Express based in West Palm Beach.
cards.body:
Spirit Airlines is liquidating its assets, including planes, airport gates and potentially its headquarters, through bankruptcy court. The disappearance of the airline leaves travelers with fewer low-cost carrier options. Treasure Coast entrepreneur LeRoy Gillead II has proposed acquiring all of Spirit, rehiring its workers and rebranding the airline as Florida Air Express, a low-cost carrier based in West Palm Beach. Court papers show Gillead is seeking up to $250 million from private investors. The deadline for bids is July.

Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, expressed skepticism about Gillead's proposal, calling it "a pie in the sky thing." Henderson said it is more likely Spirit's assets will be divided among the highest bidders, probably major airlines. Henderson noted that Frontier and Allegiant remain in the low-cost category and advised travelers to search multiple airlines for bargains using Google Flights rather than remain loyal to one carrier. "Be airline agnostic; that's the best advice I have for consumers," Henderson said. The big yellow jets Spirit was known for will likely be repainted.

hero.headline: SoFlo Market brings July 4 celebration with kids parade and patriotic events to Boca Raton City Hall
hero.teaser: The popular SoFlo Market will turn Boca Raton City Hall into a hub of red, white and blue celebration on Independence Day. The free monthly event will take place Saturday, July 4, drawing families, food lovers and local shopping enthusiasts from across Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
The SoFlo Market is transforming Boca Raton City Hall into a red, white and blue celebration this Independence Day. Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas told WPTV that the free monthly market's mission is to uplift small local businesses and bring the community together. For the holiday edition, organizers are adding patriotic touches throughout the event. Highlights include a kids parade, live DJ, unique vendors, gourmet food offerings, and free gifts for the first 20 children who arrive.

Family entertainment takes center stage with activities designed for all ages. Children can enjoy face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, and balloon twisting. The market will also feature its signature handmade crafts and desserts. A live appearance by the SoFlo Market's flamboyant flamingo mascot is expected to be a crowd favorite, adding to the festive atmosphere.

The event emphasizes community connections through local partnerships. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to participate, reinforcing the family-focused environment. Freitas' son Kyle and husband Eddie are part of the organizing team working to ensure activities run smoothly. On-site generators will power the event, and strong cell service will allow visitors to share moments instantly on social media. The market's Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and YouTube channels will feature behind-the-scenes content throughout the day.

The SoFlo Market takes place Saturday, July 4, 2026 from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Boca Raton City Hall, located at 201 West Palmetto Park Road. Admission is free. While the market runs monthly, Freitas says the Independence Day edition always stands out as a particularly special event. Independent markets like SoFlo are increasingly important to local economies, offering exposure for small businesses while creating spaces where neighbors can connect. By combining the market experience with Fourth of July traditions, organizers are making a statement of community pride. Freitas emphasized the event's importance: "We want to make people proud to call this place home."

cards.headline: Florida Mango Festival showcases 75 vendors and rare varieties Saturday in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: Florida-grown mangoes from sweet and creamy to citrusy and tropical will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beac.
cards.body:
Florida-grown mangoes from sweet and creamy to citrusy and tropical will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center. Organizers said the event will feature more than 75 vendors serving up local mango varieties, grafted trees, tropical fruits, and mango-themed products. Alex Salazar of Tropical Acres Farms told WPTV the indoor, air-conditioned venue offers an ideal setting for people to taste, learn, and discover the magic of Florida-grown mangoes without worrying about the summer heat.

Festival co-organizer Vince Rogers previewed some of the state's most unique varieties, including Fruit Cocktail, a sweet, multi-layered flavor; Orange Sherbet, offering creamy citrus notes; and Pineapple Pleasure, with tropical pineapple undertones. He said Florida hosts more than 350 mango varieties far beyond what's typically available in grocery stores. Throughout the day, visitors can attend educational talks on home mango growing and grafting techniques. Salazar will lead demonstrations offering tips to ensure success for both beginners and seasoned growers. Additional features include an ID Your Mango booth, a scion exchange for online mango community members, and a master display of Florida's diverse mango cultivars. The festival begins at 10:30 a.m., with first pick ticket holders entering at 9 a.m., at 650 Okeechobee Blvd. in West Palm Beach.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges pet owners to prepare disaster plans during hurricane season
cards.teaser: With hurricane season in full swing, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits.
cards.body:
With hurricane season now underway, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create disaster plans for their pets before the next storm arrives. Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams, told WPTV that keeping pets alongside their owners during a hurricane is the safest approach. The shelter's expert team recommends several critical preparatory steps, including ensuring pets wear collars with current identification and have updated microchips registered with correct contact information. Pet owners should introduce their animals to a designated safe room, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conduct practice runs so the hurricane is not their first time in that space.

The shelter also advises preparing a comprehensive pet emergency kit containing a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and boxes for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. Pet owners should keep a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels accessible and maintain recent photos of their pets, ideally with their owner, to assist with identification if separated. Florida's hurricane season runs June through November, overlapping with extreme summer heat, making year-round pet safety measures important.

cards.headline: Boca Raton George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, has achieved a record-breaking milestone in 2026, awarding more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund in Boca Raton awarded a record $7.5 million to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. President Tim Snow told WPTV that the nonprofit has now distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. Founded over 40 years ago, the program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college. Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted that the fund's services extend beyond financial help, providing mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast.

Scholarship recipient Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University. The fund's expanded services include the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine. The boutique offers professional, formal, and casual wear to help scholars prepare for interviews, internships, and campus life. Donations to the boutique include new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories.

hero.headline: Supreme Court Ruling Allows End to Protected Status for 350,000 Haitian Refugees, Nearly Half in Florida
hero.body:
The Supreme Court's 6-3 decision has cleared the way for the Department of Homeland Security to end temporary protected status for 350,000 Haitians across the country. Within hours of the ruling, Rep. Frederica Wilson of Miami-Dade responded by introducing the Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act in the House. The bill would create a pathway to green cards for eligible Haitian nationals who have lived in the United States since June 26, 2024, as well as their family members.

Florida will experience the effects of this decision more than any other state. According to the National Immigration Forum, approximately 404,000 TPS holders currently live in Florida, significantly more than Texas with roughly 147,000. The Migration Policy Institute reports that nearly half of all Haitians in the United States, about 49 percent, live in Florida. The Supreme Court's ruling affects Haitians who have been living legally in the country for years, many of whom registered, paid required fees, worked, paid taxes, and established roots in their communities.

Wilson, who has represented Miami-Dade for more than four decades, called the Supreme Court decision heartbreaking but emphasized that Congress retains the power to protect these families. She stated that her bill would move Haitian families from uncertainty to stability, and that TPS was never meant to become a lifetime of uncertainty. Her bill already has support from other Florida Democrats, including Reps. Maxwell Frost of Orlando and Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Broward County, who became original co-sponsors. In April, the House previously passed a separate bill to extend TPS for Haitians through a discharge petition, which received support from 10 Republicans including South Florida representatives Mario Diaz-Balart, Carlos Gimenez, and Maria Elvira Salazar.

The path forward in the Senate presents a more significant challenge. Any legislation will require 60 votes to advance, a difficult threshold even with leadership backing. Wilson argued that her bill creates a responsible pathway to lawful permanent resident status while maintaining safeguards to protect public safety. She emphasized that Haitian families have complied with legal requirements and strengthened communities by working and paying taxes. The Supreme Court's decision puts hundreds of thousands of Haitian families at risk of deportation after years of legal residence in the United States.

cards.headline: Florida Property Tax Amendment Has 64% Support But Deep Partisan Divide in New Poll
cards.teaser: A constitutional amendment to raise Florida's homestead exemption to $250,000 would likely pass if the November election were held today, with nearly two-thirds of voters supporting it, according to new polling.
cards.body:
A new Sachs Media poll shows Florida's proposed property tax amendment would likely pass if the November election were held today, with 64% overall support. However, backing fractures sharply along party lines, with 87% of Republicans supporting the measure compared with 62% of independents and 35% of Democrats. The survey of 850 Florida voters conducted June 22-24 had a 3.8-percentage-point margin of error. The amendment would exempt the first $250,000 of homestead property value from taxation on most local levies. Support cuts across homeowner and renter lines nearly identically at 65% and 64% respectively. Among homeowners, 57% said they would be more likely to stay in their current home if it passes, while 42% of renters said they would be more likely to buy a home.

State economists estimate the amendment could cost local governments $11.86 billion annually once fully implemented. By fiscal year 2028-29, counties could lose $8.775 billion in revenue. Miami-Dade County would face $445 million in cuts, while smaller rural counties dependent on homestead property taxes could lose up to 35% of their revenue. The Legislature passed the measure during a Special Session on June 2, placing it on the November 3 ballot. If approved by at least 60% of voters, homestead exemptions would progressively rise to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with subsequent increases tied to inflation.

cards.headline: Political Committee Launches Campaign to Defeat DeSantis Property Tax Overhaul
cards.teaser: A new political committee chaired by former Leon County Commissioner Bryan Desloge is raising funds to urge Floridians to reject a proposed constitutional amendment that would increase the homestead exemption to $250,000.
cards.body:
The Stop Unfair Tax Shifts PC, chaired by former Leon County Commissioner Bryan Desloge, is raising funds to oppose Amendment 3 in November's election. Desloge, a Republican who spent 14 years on the Commission before losing to a Democrat in 2020, argues that the amendment would shift costs for public safety, roads and bridges, stormwater protection and hurricane response to residents and businesses. "The consequences of Amendment 3 will shift those bills, causing higher rent, more expensive everyday purchases, costlier first homes, and many small businesses that can't absorb an increase in commercial property taxes," Desloge said. The committee contends voters are being asked to approve a complex package of tax changes with major consequences for Florida.

If approved by at least 60 percent of voters, the amendment would raise the homestead exemption on primary residences to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, then tie further increases to the consumer price index. Newer residents would qualify for a $50,000 exemption initially, reaching the full benefit after five years of Florida residency. The amendment would also cap annual assessment increases on non-homestead property at 5 percent, down from 10 percent. The Office of Economic and Demographic Research estimates roughly $11.86 billion would eventually be drained from local budgets annually. St. Lucie could lose 35 percent of its revenue, while Miami-Dade would see a $445 million decrease by Fiscal Year 2028-29.

cards.headline: Trump Approval Rating Sinks Underwater in Florida as Midterms Approach
cards.teaser: New polling shows President Donald Trump's approval rating has turned negative in his home state of Florida, with 52% of voters viewing him unfavorably compared to 46% who see him positively.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump's approval rating has declined significantly in Florida, according to new polling from Global Strategy Group. The survey shows 52% of Florida voters view Trump unfavorably compared to 46% who see him positively, marking a 10-point swing from January when he held a net positive rating. The poll was released by Democratic Senate candidate Alex Vindman's campaign as he argues Florida could be competitive when U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody faces voters in November. A GSG polling memo states the "double-digit decline in Trump's popularity has created a more favorable political environment for Democrats in 2026, despite Florida's partisan dynamics."

The decline extends across multiple voter groups. Support among white college-aged voters dropped 15 points since January, while registered Republicans saw a net 10-point decline in approval. Even among self-identified Trump 2024 voters, his numbers fell by 10 points. Trump's approval rating has also turned negative in other key states: Ohio shows 41% approval and 53% disapproval, while Texas reflects 41% to 54%. A May GSG poll showed Moody holding a 46% to 43% lead over Vindman, within the poll's 3.1% margin of error. In 2018, the last midterm during Trump's presidency, he held a positive rating in Florida as Rick Scott defeated Democratic Sen. Bill Nelson.

cards.headline: DeSantis Signs Law Creating Felony for Rental Application Fraud in Florida
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed HB 1293 into law earlier this month, creating a new third-degree felony for people who knowingly gain access to residential housing through false statements, forged documents or identity misrepresentation.
cards.body:
The Florida Apartment Association is celebrating the passage of HB 1293, a new law signed by Gov. Ron DeSantis on June 12 that creates a third-degree felony for rental application fraud. The bill passed unanimously in both chambers and goes into effect Oct. 1. The law targets people who knowingly and willfully gain access to residential housing through materially false statements, forged documents, counterfeit records, or identity misrepresentation. The FAA identified the growing problem, worked with industry stakeholders to develop a policy solution, and championed the legislation throughout the legislative process. The issue is particularly a problem in the Miami-Fort Lauderdale area, where people use altered pay stubs, false employment records, synthetic identities, and counterfeit bank statements to lie on rental applications.

The consequences of rental application fraud extend beyond housing providers, according to the FAA. When fraudsters obtain affordable housing units for which they are not eligible, they reduce access for working families and individuals who legitimately qualify for those limited units. Tenants who commit application fraud often default on rent, leading to costly legal proceedings and financial losses that affect housing operations and affordability. The new legislation also makes application fraud a lease violation, allowing a tenant's lease to be terminated legally through existing legal processes. "Florida has become one of the nation's hotspots for rental application fraud, creating significant challenges for housing providers," said Amanda White, Vice President of the Florida Apartment Association.

cards.headline: DEA's Miami Lab Warns of Alarming Rise in Fentanyl and Carfentanil in Florida Drug Samples
cards.teaser: Forensic chemists at the DEA's busiest drug lab in Miami are seeing fentanyl and carfentanil show up in alarming numbers, with one recent sample testing at 16% fentanyl and also containing carfentanil.
cards.body:
DEA lab chemist Alyssa Sanchez, who has tested drugs at Miami's busiest drug lab for the last three years, said the amount of fentanyl and carfentanil she is seeing in recent samples is alarming and new. A fentanyl kilo brick recently tested contained about 16 percent fentanyl and also contained carfentanil, a tranquilizer for large animals such as elephants with no approved human use. Carfentanil is a multitude of times more potent than fentanyl, which is 100 times stronger than morphine and 50 times stronger than heroin. According to the DEA and CDC, fentanyl is now the leading cause of death for adults ages 18 to 45. As little as 2 milligrams of fentanyl, roughly the size of a grain of salt, can be deadly.

Miles Aley, special agent in charge of the DEA's Miami Division, said after the Chinese government banned precursor chemicals used to make fentanyl, Mexican drug cartels began resorting to carfentanil to make fentanyl and other drugs more potent. The cartels obtained chemicals and expertise through the dark web. While fentanyl and carfentanil overdose deaths remain down from a decade ago, Aley warned that more people are surviving overdoses because of Narcan, an over-the-counter nasal spray that reverses opioid overdose effects, meaning lower death counts do not necessarily reflect lower use. Aley also warned that new drugs resistant to Narcan are now appearing. Next month, the DEA will host its inaugural Fentanyl Free America Summit in Orlando to raise public awareness about the dangers of the latest fentanyl crisis.

cards.headline: DeSantis Approves Charlie Kirk Memorial Avenue at FIU, Trump Boulevard in Broward
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed legislation renaming a 1-mile stretch of roadway alongside Florida International University after slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk and part of Commercial Boulevard in Broward County as President Donald J. Trump Boulevard.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed HB 33 by Miami Rep. Juan Porras, which renames a 1-mile stretch of Southwest 107th Avenue in west Miami-Dade County between Coral Way and Tamiami Trail as "Charlie Kirk Memorial Avenue." The measure passed on party-line votes in both chambers, with Doral Sen. Ana Maria Rodriguez carrying a companion bill. It also authorizes renaming part of Commercial Boulevard in Broward County as "President Donald J. Trump Boulevard," implementing a resolution Lauderdale-by-the-Sea narrowly passed in October. Porras said the FIU location is appropriate since Kirk helped found Florida's first Turning Point USA chapter there in 2015. A House staff analysis estimates total implementation costs at $4,800, or $1,200 per sign for two signs per designation. The designations are honorary and do not require changes to local street signs, addresses, or 911 systems. HB 33 takes effect July 1.

Opponents argued Kirk, who owned a vacation home in Longboat Key in Sarasota County, had little tangible connection to Florida or Miami-Dade. They cited his rhetoric, including questions about Black pilots' qualifications, references to "prowling Blacks" targeting white people in urban areas, and his perpetuation of the "great replacement theory." During the final committee hearing, St. Petersburg Democratic Rep. Michele Rayner quoted Kirk calling Martin Luther King Jr. "awful" and George Floyd a "scumbag," and recited statements Kirk made about accomplished Black women. Miami Democratic Rep. Ashley Gantt called Kirk "mediocre and racist" during House floor debate in February. Kirk was shot and killed by a lone sniper on a Utah university campus in September.

cards.headline: Fentanyl and carfentanil appear in rising numbers at Florida DEA lab
cards.teaser: DEA chemist Alyssa Sanchez reports alarming increases in fentanyl and carfentanil samples at the Miami lab, with some samples containing both deadly substances.
cards.body:
The DEA's Miami drug lab, considered the busiest in America due to its coastal location and proximity to South America, is detecting fentanyl and carfentanil in alarming numbers. "I see a lot of fentanyl, but even more recently I've seen a lot of carfentanil in my samples; it's scary!" said DEA lab chemist Alyssa Sanchez. In one sample, a kilogram brick tested at approximately 16 percent fentanyl and also contained carfentanil, which is multitudes of times more potent than fentanyl. Sanchez has been testing drugs at the lab for three years and said the amount she is seeing in recent samples is new for her. According to the DEA and CDC, fentanyl is now the leading cause of death for adults ages 18 to 45, with as little as 2 milligrams capable of being deadly.

After the Chinese government banned precursor chemicals used to make fentanyl, Mexican drug cartels began resorting to carfentanil, which has no approved human use and is a tranquilizer for large animals such as elephants. Miles Aley, special agent in charge of the DEA's Miami Division, said cartels obtained chemicals and expertise through the dark web. Aley also warned that new drugs are now appearing that are resistant to Narcan. Next month, the DEA will host its inaugural Fentanyl Free America Summit in Orlando to raise public awareness about the dangers of the current fentanyl crisis.
